name: Yalaku
world_status: statement found in a copy already on file

earlier_scan.source_named: Aikhenvald, Alexandra Y. 2023. A Grammar of Yalaku (Brill); full grammar with phonology chapter, paywalled/not openly readable.

new_statements.quote: Yalaku has one primary stress. Stress is realized through increased intensity of the vowel, and is contrastive. Minimal pairs include: héña 'be able to, possible' versus heñá 'day after tomorrow' wosék 'small, little' versus ... [p. 152] ... Stress is only partly predictable. In polysyllabic words, syllables of CVC structure tend to attract stress. In morphologically complex words, stress placement depends on the properties of the affix. For instance, the allative-accusative case marker -re is not stressed, e.g. horóbu-re 'to men's house'. In contrast, the locative case -bu is stressed, e.g. horòbu ... [p. 153] ... secondary stress per word, in addition to the primary stress. There are no unstressed function words
new_statements.citation: Aikhenvald, Alexandra Y. 2020. Word in Yalaku. In Alexandra Y. Aikhenvald, R. M. W. Dixon & Nathan M. White (eds), Phonological Word and Grammatical Word: A Cross-Linguistic Typology, 147-175. Oxford: Oxford University Press. DOI 10.1093/oso/9780198865681.003.0006
new_statements.locator: §3.1 'Stress as a prosodic feature', pp. 152-153 (Google Books page codes PA152, PA153); summary §6
new_statements.rule_in_words: One primary stress per phonological word; its position is contrastive and only partly predictable (minimal pairs differ by stress on first vs second syllable). Tendency: in polysyllabic words a closed CVC syllable attracts stress; in morphologically complex words placement depends on the affix (some case markers such as -re never take stress, others such as locative -bu do). In rapid speech, when a monosyllabic word cliticises to a preceding host the resulting word takes final stress if it is no longer than four syllables (p. 153 snippet, q7).
new_statements.secondary_stress: One secondary stress per word, in addition to the primary stress (p. 153; snippet q6 truncates the start of the sentence).
new_statements.exceptions: Affix-dependent placement (-re unstressed vs -bu stressed); five disyllabic modality/aspect markers attach to the root but form a phonological word of their own; proclitics cannot carry primary stress; no unstressed function words.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (the chapter's topic); the four-syllable final-stress rule concerns rapid-speech cliticisation of noun-phrase sequences, not citation forms.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Yalaku as spoken in Yalaku (Yelogu) village, Washkuk Mountains north of Ambunti, East Sepik — the same variety as Glottolog yelo1243 (Laycock's 'Yelogu' /yAlAkw/ = Aikhenvald's 'Yalaku'). No dialect issue. Laycock's Wosera stress rules (Abelam/Ambulas, abel1240 area) are a different language and are not used here.
